newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - U.S. Robotics defends deal value.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - U.S. Robotics defends deal value.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp chairman and chief executive Casey Cowell on Thursday rebuffed comments that his company's proposed merger with computer network leader 3Com Corp did not reflect the company's value.
"We're running the business very aggressively for our shareholders today and for the future," Cowell said in an interview, adding the sale price was "absolutely" not too low.
"The objective is to gain share over the long term and be well positioned for future technologies over the next few years," Cowell said. "That's the real issue."

Cowell pointed out that valuations of networking companies have been very volatile recently, adding that both U.S. Robotics and 3Com share prices have declined recently. 3Com especially has been under pressure after announcing its fiscal third quarter revenues would be weaker and that it cut prices on its core product, its adapter cards.
"What we were really interested in...is that going forward Robotics shareholders have a little under 50 percent of the combined company, so we feel comfortable with that," he said.

Late Wednesday, U.S. Robotics and 3Com said they signed a definitive agreement to merge in a deal valued at $7.3 billion, including outstanding shares and options. Each U.S. Robotics share will be exchanged for 1.75 3Com shares, regardless of the price at the time of closing. The name of the combined company will be 3Com.

Some analysts said the U.S. Robotics was worth anywhere from $75 to $90 a share. According to Tuesday's closing price, used to figure the value of the deal, each U.S. Robotics share was priced at $68.47.
"Looking at value, it's one instantaneous position today," Cowell said. "The real objective was to position our company and our shareholders well for the next several years."
Cowell said U.S. Robotics approached 3Com to explore the possibility of 3Com becoming a partner in x2, its new 56 kilobit per second modem technology which began shipping earlier this week.
U.S. Robotics wanted to work closely with 3Com "with merging being a distinct possibility", he said.
"We're going to sell a lot of x2 on our own, and we think that we'll sell even more x2 combined with 3Com," Cowell said.
The merger is expected to close in summer.

In the longer term, Cowell said 3Com will bring the combined company into the corporate market, currently not a U.S. Robotics strength, and give it local area network (LAN) technology. This is important as new digital subscriber line and cable technology take hold in the market, he said.
"We felt that to really be able to be the top performer in those technological areas, we were really looking for a way to provide a LAN-to-WAN (wide area network) solution," he said.
Although he expects the merger to make a more efficient combined company, Cowell said he does not expect any job cuts.
"I don't expect there to be any job cuts, but you can't say with absolute certainty that not one job will be cut," he said. "The whole purpose of this merger is growth in the future."
Cowell, who was named vice chairman of the combined 3Com, said he will still have direct involvement in the company.
"I am a major stockholder of Robotics and I will soon be a major stockholder of 3Com," Cowell said. "I have a long-term employment agreement and look forward to being a part of this organization."
